analysis.one_liner: Raises the minimum wage to $6.15 over two years while exempting some tech, sales, and funeral workers from wage and overtime rules.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote and died at the end of the 106th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have raised the federal minimum wage from $5.15 to $5.48 in 2000, $5.81 in 2001, and $6.15 by 2002. At the same time, it would have expanded the existing overtime exemption for computer professionals to cover network and database analysts, created a new exemption for certain technical sales employees, and exempted licensed funeral directors and embalmers from minimum wage and overtime rules entirely. It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, sent to a subcommittee, and never received a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers earning the federal minimum wage would have gotten three raises totaling $1.00 an hour by 2002. Tech employers, employers of technical sales staff, and the funeral industry would have gained new exemptions from minimum wage and overtime obligations for some of their workers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-wage workers, plus some tech and funeral employers

how_it_helps.text: It would have raised the federal minimum wage from $5.15 to $5.48 in April 2000, $5.81 in April 2001, and $6.15 in April 2002.
The wage increases would have applied to workers covered by the Fair Labor Standards Act, which sets the wage floor for most hourly employees.
It would have expanded the computer-professional exemption to hourly workers paid at least $27.63 an hour, giving employers of network and database analysts more flexibility.

analysis.who_pays: Employers paying the minimum wage would have borne the higher payroll costs. Workers in the newly exempted categories — certain computer professionals, technical sales employees, and funeral directors and embalmers — would have lost overtime and, for funeral workers, minimum wage protections.
analysis.who_pays_short: Minimum-wage employers; some tech, sales, funeral workers

drawbacks.text: The bill carved new groups out of overtime protection: technical sales employees meeting its criteria would no longer earn time-and-a-half for long hours, and licensed funeral directors and embalmers would lose both minimum wage and overtime coverage entirely.

The computer-professional exemption would have been broadened to cover network and database analysts and developers, extending a wage-and-overtime carve-out to more of the fast-growing tech workforce.
The wage increase was gradual — reaching $6.15 only in April 2002 — and $6.15 was a modest target for that era's minimum wage debates.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The wage increase was real but modest and phased in over two years, and it came bundled with exemptions that eroded overtime protections for some skilled workers — a trade-off that tech, sales, and funeral employers would have welcomed. An honest reading is that the bill gave a raise with one hand and took protections away with the other.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, then to a subcommittee, and it died there without ever being voted on.

narrative.text: Rep. John Shimkus (R-IL) introduced the bill on March 6, 2000.

The House referred it to the Committee on Education and the Workforce, which referred it to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections three weeks later; no markup, floor vote, or further action followed before the 106th Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers came out ahead: they avoided both the $1.00-an-hour wage increase and, since the bill died whole, none of its new exemptions took effect either. Low-wage workers got no raise.

for.name: Rep. John Shimkus
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill; it received no cosponsors.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections and never scheduled a markup or sent it to the floor; it expired in committee.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors, so the record shows no pattern of party support or opposition; a Republican introduced it and a Republican-controlled committee let it lapse.

industries.note: The bill would have broadened the computer-professional overtime exemption to cover network and database analysts, designers, and developers paid at least $27.63 an hour, letting employers of those workers skip overtime pay. Since the bill died, employers also avoided the minimum wage increase — which would have raised their payroll costs.
Licensed funeral directors and embalmers would have been fully exempt from minimum wage and overtime requirements. The bill never passed, so no exemption took effect.

A new exemption would have removed minimum wage and overtime protections from technical sales employees meeting detailed compensation criteria, letting employers put them on commission-style pay without overtime. The bill died before this took effect.

A $1.00-an-hour increase phased over two years would have raised payroll costs for businesses paying the wage floor, particularly low-wage service employers. Because the bill died, these costs never materialized.
